<description>
This is a follow-up to [#35728](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35728#issuecomment-6214014188).

While reviewing that PR, I noticed that `FindTx()` could return `nullopt` even when LevelDB had encountered an error. I first confirmed that a transaction could be retrieved, then deliberately damaged part of the test’s temporary txindex database. LevelDB detected the corruption, but the same lookup returned `nullopt` instead of throwing. Restoring the original data made the lookup work again.

The candidate scan checks whether the iterator has a valid entry, but it does not check its error status. An invalid iterator can mean that the scan reached the end normally, or that it stopped because of a database error. This means a failed scan can be treated as an ordinary missing transaction.

This adds `CDBIterator::CheckStatus()` and calls it after the candidate scan, before choosing a result. Any iterator error goes through the existing `HandleError()` path and throws `dbwrapper_error`. A normal missing transaction still returns `nullopt`.

I added a reproducer on [my branch](https://github.com/musaHaruna/bitcoin/tree/txindex-iterator-error-repro). The first commit adds a test that fails before the fix. The second commit applies the fix, and the same test passes.
</description>

[2026-11-10] c:6772962317 comment by andrewtoth (member):
The same issue exists for any consumer using iterators. Should we instead check status and throw inside `Seek` and `Next`? Would there be a noticeable performance penalty?
[2026-11-11] c:6805524926 comment by musaHaruna (contributor):
[quoted text omitted]

If I understand the code path correctly, I think adding the check inside `Seek()` and `Next()` would do more than check a single error flag. `DBIter::status()` delegates to its internal iterator when its own status is OK. When that is a merging iterator, `MergingIterator::status()` loops over its children, which can also check their underlying iterators. On the healthy path, it checks every child.

Putting this inside `Next()` would repeat that work for every entry. For a scan of one million entries, that means about one million status checks, plus the initial seek check. With the approach used in `FindTx()`, we check status once after the candidate scan, before using the results. LevelDB records errors encountered during iteration, so the final check can still report them. It also needs to run when `Valid()` is true, since an iterator can skip a damaged block and remain valid.

I also compared both approaches using `bench_bitcoin`. The shared version checks inside `Seek()`, `SeekToFirst()`, and `Next()`. For the disk key/value scan, six paired runs showed a median **11.90% increase in time**, ranging from 11.47% to 13.03%. That was roughly **144 ms versus 161 ms for one million entries**.

| Pair | Check after scan, ns/entry | Check after each movement, ns/entry | Time change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 144.193 | 162.981 | +13.03% |
| 2 | 144.417 | 160.984 | +11.47% |
| 3 | 143.856 | 160.444 | +11.53% |
| 4 | 144.238 | 162.455 | +12.63% |
| 5 | 143.861 | 161.503 | +12.26% |
| 6 | 143.624 | 160.162 | +11.51% |

I ran the benchmarks on an Apple M5 with 16 GiB of RAM.

So I think the extra work is measurable for these scans. Checking inside the movement functions would protect callers automatically, but we could also use explicit checks for the other callers, making sure early returns check status and single-seek callers check after the seek. That would include callers such as `IsEmpty()`, `NeedsUpgrade()`, `FindSpender()`, and the UTXO cursor consumers. If this approach is desirable, I can extend this PR to cover them too.
</new_statements>
